## Where jets get their power {#cosmic-messengers}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Tidal disruption

<video class="slide-video media-height-lg" style="--media-max-height: 620px;" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" poster="media/jets/jet_launch_en.jpg" src="media/jets/jet_launch_en.mp4" aria-label="From a star to a jet: tidal disruption, returning debris and a schematic magnetic engine."></video>

::: {.media-caption}
Computed debris orbits, schematic magnetic engine.
:::

### AGN

Gas feeds an accretion disc around a supermassive black hole.

Magnetic fields can extract rotational energy and carry it into a jet.

The gas supply can sustain activity beyond a single stellar disruption.

**Blazars:** the jet points close to our line of sight.

::: {.media-caption}
[Blandford, Meier & Readhead, Relativistic Jets in AGN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.06025)
:::

### Gamma-ray bursts

| Scenario | Fuel for the central engine |
| --- | --- |
| Massive-star collapse | Stellar material falls onto the compact remnant. |
| Compact-object merger | Debris forms a temporary accretion disc. |

Accretion onto a black hole or the spin of a strongly magnetized neutron star
can power a relativistic outflow.

The engine operates during a transient event.

::: {.media-caption}
[P. Mészáros, Gamma-Ray Bursts](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0605208)
:::

### Cosmic messengers

Charged cosmic rays bend in magnetic fields.

Photons can scatter or be absorbed.

Neutrinos can escape dense environments and preserve directional information.

:::

::: {.notes}
Source physics occupies 21–28 minutes. Allow about two minutes here, including
the complete 98.4-second English film. The main question is where the jet's
power comes from. Follow the tidal disruption, returning debris, accretion
disc and magnetic extraction of rotational energy. The last part shows bulk
plasma acceleration, not a calculation of a non-thermal proton spectrum.

This is a jetted tidal-disruption example, not the origin of every AGN jet.
The debris follows computed test-particle orbits in a frozen-in approximation
with an apsidal-precession prescription. The disc and magnetic engine are
schematic, not a GRMHD simulation. The Swift J1644+57 curve is a schematic
trend, not plotted observational data. Avoid suggesting that every tidal
disruption launches a jet.

The next film changes scenario: a different star enters a jet that already
exists. It is not a continuation of the disrupted star's trajectory.
The optional Cosmic messengers tab retains the comparison between charged
particles, photons and neutrinos. State the energy range and avoid suggesting
unlimited neutrino transparency at every energy and column depth.

The static AGN and Gamma-ray bursts tabs show alternative engine contexts,
not additional stages of the tidal-disruption film. In an AGN, gas accretion
can supply the disc without a tidal disruption. Only a subset of AGN produces
powerful jets. Viewing angle defines a blazar, not a different power source.
For GRBs, collapse and compact-object mergers provide different fuel supplies.
Black-hole accretion and magnetar spin-down are model alternatives, not a claim
that both engines operate in every burst. Burst duration alone does not identify
the progenitor. The static tabs compare different engine fuel supplies.

References for the static engine tabs:
[Blandford, Meier and Readhead](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.06025) and
[Mészáros](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0605208).

## How jets produce neutrinos {#acceleration-and-confinement}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Star in the jet

<video class="slide-video media-height-lg" style="--media-max-height: 620px;" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" poster="media/jets/jet_star_en.jpg" src="media/jets/jet_star_en.mp4" aria-label="A star in an existing jet: a gas shock and stripped cloud, schematic proton acceleration and neutrino production."></video>

::: {.media-caption}
Scenario and calculation: [Barkov, Aharonian & Bosch-Ramon (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.5252) · The film illustrates the idea: simplified gas model, schematic protons and neutrinos
:::

### Gas

Accelerated protons collide with nuclei in dense gas.

$$
pp\longrightarrow\pi^{\pm},\,\pi^0+X
$$

**Possible targets:** a stripped stellar envelope or a gas cloud in the jet.

The gas density and the proton residence time control the interaction yield.

::: {.media-caption}
[Wang et al., jet–cloud/star scenario](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00601)
:::

### Photons

Accelerated protons interact with a radiation field.

$$
p\gamma\longrightarrow\pi^{\pm},\,\pi^0+X
$$

**Possible targets:** synchrotron photons in the jet, or photons from the
accretion disc and its surroundings.

The pion-production threshold depends on photon energy and collision angle.

::: {.media-caption}
[Murase & Stecker, High-Energy Neutrinos from AGN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03381)
:::

### Confinement

The jet supplies energy. The star creates a shock and a dense target.

$$
r_L=\frac{p}{ZeB}\lesssim R
$$

A source must retain particles long enough to accelerate them.

Energy losses and the available time also limit the maximum energy.

### Converter

![](media/theory/converter-cycle.svg){.slide-media .nostretch style="--media-width: 1400px; --media-max-height: 525px;" fig-alt="Schematic of one converter acceleration cycle: a proton in a relativistic jet becomes a neutron, leaves the jet without feeling the magnetic field, becomes a proton again outside and is turned back into the jet by the field, gaining energy of order Gamma squared. Each conversion also emits a neutrino. Paths are illustrative."}

::: {.media-caption}
Charge changes let particles cross the field · Gain $\sim\Gamma^2$ per cycle · [Derishev et al. (2003)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0301263)
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
**Say:** A star that wanders into a jet is like a rock in a fast river: a shock forms in front of it, protons are accelerated there and hit the star's torn-off gas, and those collisions make neutrinos. The idea and the real calculation are by Barkov, Aharonian and Bosch-Ramon; our film only illustrates it.

Scenario and calculation:
[Barkov, Aharonian and Bosch-Ramon, ApJ 724, 1517 (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.5252).
They solved the hydrodynamics of a red-giant envelope blown by an AGN jet near
its base, and proposed proton–proton collisions in the shocked material as the
origin of day-scale TeV flares from M87. Their paper addresses gamma-ray
flares; the same pp collisions also make charged pions and hence neutrinos,
which is the step this lecture emphasizes. Barkov's own calculation movies are
not shown. Say explicitly that the film illustrates the idea and that the exact
calculation belongs to Barkov and co-authors.

Allow about two minutes here, including the complete 97.4-second English
film. A star with a wind enters a pre-existing jet. A shock forms and dense
material is stripped downstream. Follow the highlighted proton through
repeated shock crossings, then its collision in the cloud. Pion production
and decay supply the transition to the next slide.

The gas comes from DN's axisymmetric, non-relativistic hydrodynamic calculation
of a dense cloud with a wind in a supersonic flow, with density contrast 100.
It has no self-gravity or resolved stellar structure and is not a relativistic
AGN-jet calculation. The remaining-material counter tracks dense tracer
material in this model, not the surviving core mass of a real star.
Proton acceleration, collisions, gamma-ray absorption and neutrino rays are
schematic overlays. Their displayed counts are not a predicted neutrino flux.

The cloud example uses $n=10^{10}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$,
$R=10^{14}\,\mathrm{cm}$, $\sigma_{pp}=50\,\mathrm{mb}$ and $\kappa=0.5$.
Thus $\tau_{pp}=n\sigma_{pp}R=0.05$ and the thin-target energy-loss estimate
for one crossing is $\kappa\tau_{pp}\simeq2.5\%$.
This is the proton energy going into pion production, not the fraction
carried by neutrinos. A longer residence time can increase the yield.
The film introduces starlight as a possible $p\gamma$ target at sufficiently
high energies without calculating its efficiency. Gamma-ray attenuation is
illustrative rather than a radiative-transfer result.

The displayed gyroradius uses SI units for momentum, magnetic field and charge.
The confinement condition is necessary, but not sufficient for acceleration.

Converter tab
([Derishev, Aharonian, Kocharovsky and Kocharovsky, PRD 68, 043003 (2003)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0301263)):
in a relativistic flow, charge-changing reactions ($p\gamma\to n\pi^+$ and back,
or $e^\pm\leftrightarrow\gamma$; also inelastic nucleon–nucleon collisions) let
a particle leave the flow as a neutral that ignores the magnetic field and
return as a charged particle deflected by the ambient field. The paper states
an energy gain roughly equal to the bulk Lorentz factor squared per cycle.
A flux-weighted Monte Carlo for a planar boundary gives a mean gain of about
$2.7\,\Gamma^2$ for $\Gamma=3$–30; the factor depends on geometry, hence
"$\sim\Gamma^2$". Compare a non-relativistic shock, where the fractional gain per
crossing is only of order the shock speed over $c$. The mechanism needs intense
radiation fields (or dense gas); the cycle does not always close, and losses and
feedback on the flow limit it. For nucleons the authors note that it routinely
produces high-energy neutrinos at about 50% relative efficiency. The diagram
shows one illustrative cycle; no rate or spectrum is computed. Generator:
`assets/theory/converter_cycle.py`.

The Gas and Photons tabs are static comparisons of hadronuclear and
photomeson production. The inclusive equations describe pion populations,
not every charge in each collision. Real sources may have both target types.
Which dominates depends on target density, spectra, particle energy and
residence time. Do not infer a neutrino luminosity from these schematic channels.
The photon energies and collision angles entering the threshold must be
evaluated in a common local frame. Synchrotron and external photon fields are
alternative jet targets discussed by
[Murase and Stecker](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03381).
The decay chains follow next; photon propagation returns after the measured spectrum.

Film supplied by DN: `dvnanima/jet_star/media/jet_star_en.mp4`.
Model/configuration: `jet_star.py`, `hydro2d.py`, `star_physics.py`,
`config.toml` and `texts.toml` in that directory. Static poster: 56 s.
Full provenance: `media/jets/SOURCES.md`.

Original scenario: [Barkov, Aharonian & Bosch-Ramon (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.5252).
Later work: [Wang et al., jet–cloud/star interpretation of TXS 0506+056](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00601);
Fichet de Clairfontaine et al., A&A 693, A270 (2025).
Treat this as a proposed production mechanism, not an established explanation
of an observed neutrino source.
:::

## Three messengers, one energy budget {#energy-budget}

**Gamma rays, neutrinos and the most energetic cosmic rays carry similar power.**

![](media/theory/energy-budget.svg){.slide-media .nostretch style="--media-max-height: 560px;" fig-alt="Energy flux E squared times flux versus particle energy from 0.1 GeV to 200 EeV. Fermi-LAT isotropic gamma-ray background points from 0.1 to 820 GeV, the IceCube astrophysical neutrino spectrum per flavour from about 14 TeV to 5 PeV with its 68 percent band, and Pierre Auger cosmic-ray points above 3 EeV. A dashed band shows the Waxman-Bahcall bound per flavour, 0.45 to 2.25 times 1e-8; the neutrino flux reaches it near 100 TeV."}

::: {.media-caption}
Neutrinos per flavour · [Fermi-LAT (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3696) · [IceCube (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22233v3), band digitized from Fig. 3 · [Auger (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.06486) · Bound: [Waxman & Bahcall (1999)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9807282)
:::

::: {.notes}
**Say:** Put the three messengers on one scale: gamma rays, neutrinos and the highest-energy cosmic rays bring us roughly the same power per energy decade, so one family of cosmic accelerators could be feeding all three — and the neutrinos are already as bright as cosmic rays allow.

Allow about 90 seconds. The vertical axis is energy flux per logarithmic energy
interval, $E^2\Phi$, averaged over the sky. Gold: Fermi-LAT isotropic gamma-ray
background (IGRB), foreground model A, 100 MeV–820 GeV, Table 3 of Ackermann et
al., ApJ 799, 86 (2015); shaded boxes are the foreground-model range, the last
bin is an upper limit. Cyan: IceCube Combined-Fit broken power law, per flavour,
$\nu+\bar\nu$, from Table III of PRL 136, 121002 (2026); the 68% band and its
sensitive energy range are digitized from Fig. 3. The all-flavour flux is three
times higher. Orange: Pierre Auger spectrum above $2.5\times10^{18}$ eV, all
nuclei, Table VI of PRD 102, 062005 (2020), with statistical errors and 90%
upper limits.

Waxman–Bahcall bound (PRD 59, 023002 (1999)): the ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray
generation rate, $E^2\,d\dot N/dE\approx10^{44}$ erg Mpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$ in
their Eq. (1), caps the neutrino flux from the same sources if those sources are
transparent to their protons:
$I_{\max}\approx\tfrac14\xi_Z t_H\frac{c}{4\pi}E^2\,d\dot N/dE\approx1.5\times10^{-8}\xi_Z$
GeV cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$ for $\nu_\mu+\bar\nu_\mu$, with
$\xi_Z\approx0.6$ for no source evolution and $\approx3$ for QSO/star-formation-like
evolution. After oscillations the per-flavour value is $\tfrac12I_{\max}$:
$0.45$–$2.25\times10^{-8}$, the drawn band. It applies to sources not much larger
than the proton interaction length; sources opaque to cosmic rays are not bound.
Extending it down to 100 TeV assumes an $E^{-2}$ generation spectrum.

The IceCube per-flavour flux at 100 TeV is $1.77\times10^{-8}$ GeV cm$^{-2}$
s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$, inside the band. Either the sources convert a large
fraction of their proton energy into pions, or there are more sources at lower
energies, or the neutrino sources are not the ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray
sources. The comparable energy densities suggest, but do not prove, a common
origin (Ahlers & Halzen, PPNP 102, 73 (2018), Fig. 9, shows the same comparison
with older data). Different particle types and different energy ranges are
compared; the IGRB excludes resolved gamma-ray sources. The photons that
accompany the neutrinos cascade down into the Fermi band; this is quantified on
the gamma-ray budget slide after the measured spectrum.

Russian-language review for the source slides:
[С. В. Троицкий, УФН 194, 371 (2024); Phys. Usp. 67, 349](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.00281).

Generator, table excerpts, digitizer and tests: `assets/theory/`.
Figure provenance: `media/theory/SOURCES.md`.

## Production environments {#source-populations}

| Environment | Target for energetic hadrons | Observational test |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Galactic disk | Interstellar gas | Spatially extended emission |
| AGN jet | Gas or radiation | Direction and variability |
| AGN corona (hidden core) | Gas and X-ray photons | Neutrinos brighter than GeV–TeV gamma rays |
| Star-forming environment | Dense gas | Population and diffuse-flux constraints |
| GRB or tidal disruption | Gas or radiation | Time-dependent searches |

**Many faint sources:** the brightest neutrino sources seen so far supply only a
small part of the diffuse flux, so most of it should come from many faint emitters.

::: {.media-caption}
[Murase & Stecker](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03381) · Coronae: [Kheirandish, Murase & Kimura (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04475) · Populations: [Groth & Ahlers (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07718)
:::

::: {.notes}
**Say:** Neutrinos can be made wherever fast protons meet gas or light — in our Galaxy, in jets, in the hot corona right next to a black hole — and the corona is special because it lets neutrinos out while it swallows the gamma rays; and since no single source outshines the rest, we are probably seeing a crowd of faint ones.

Source physics occupies 21–28 minutes, including both jet films. Spend about
45 seconds on this table. The two jet examples are specific physical scenarios.
They do not establish that jets dominate the diffuse neutrino flux. Energetic
hadrons, target densities and residence times determine pion production.
A source class or a target field is not itself evidence of neutrino emission.

The Galactic plane constrains distributed emission, while source catalogues
and time-dependent searches ask different questions. Compact AGN regions will
be discussed again after the diffuse gamma-ray budget and at NGC 1068.
A population contribution also depends on its luminosity function and evolution.
Star-forming environments and transient models remain hypotheses tested by
measurements and upper limits; no detection of every listed class is claimed.

Hidden sources and coronae: in the disk–corona model of
[Kheirandish, Murase and Kimura, ApJ 922, 45 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04475),
protons accelerated by magnetic reconnection and/or turbulence in the magnetized
X-ray corona produce neutrinos and soft gamma rays. GeV–TeV photons are absorbed
in the dense X-ray field ($\gamma\gamma\to e^+e^-$; head-on threshold about
0.26 GeV for 1 keV target photons). They found NGC 1068 to be the most promising Seyfert galaxy
in the Northern sky and argued that hidden cores of supermassive black holes may
dominate the high-energy neutrino emission. This is a model interpretation, tested
at NGC 1068 and the gamma-ray budget slides.

Population constraints:
[Groth and Ahlers, PRD 111, 103052 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07718)
review how the non-detection of a dominant bright source constrains extragalactic
populations with general luminosity functions. The diffuse flux most likely comes
from many sources that are individually too faint to stand out. Combined searches
of the brightest sources (weighted stacking, or non-Poissonian fluctuations in
event-count histograms) can improve the discovery potential by a factor of 2–3
relative to the brightest source alone. The slide's "small part" refers to the
measured NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane fluxes, which lie well below the diffuse
flux (IceCube, PRL 136, 121002 (2026), Fig. 3).

Russian-language review:
[С. В. Троицкий, УФН 194, 371 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.00281).

Sources: [Murase & Stecker](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03381),
[D'Ammando](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.30764),
[Spiering](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.26436).
:::
